title: The Importance of Being Earnest: A Trivial Comedy for Serious People
description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 14 February 1895 and the most perfect English comedy of the nineteenth century: the comedy of two young men who both invent a fictitious invalid in order to escape their social duties, and of the women who love them for a name.
plot_or_argument: Algernon Moncrieff invents 'Bunbury', Ernest Worthing invents his invalid brother Ernest; Gwendolen Fairfax and Cecily Cardew both believe they are engaged to a man named Ernest, the engagements collapse on the discovery of the invention, and the play resolves when it appears that Jack was in fact christened Ernest and is Algernon's elder brother.
narrative_structure: Three acts, one set in a London flat and two in a Hertfordshire garden. The action is divided into three acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: John Worthing (Jack); Algernon Moncrieff; Gwendolen Fairfax; Cecily Cardew; Lady Bracknell; Miss Prism; Rev. Canon Chasuble; Lane; Merriman
literary_form: Comedy in three acts; problem play
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the marriage market, the country-house weekend, and the aesthetic and dandy culture of London. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and first performed in St James's Theatre, London, 14 February 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: The Importance of Being Earnest is the greatest English stage comedy since the Restoration and the definitive statement of Wilde's comic method: the epigram as a weapon against Victorian earnestness, and the pun on a name as the engine of a plot.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First produced at the St James's Theatre, London, on 14 February 1895 under the management of George Alexander, and published by Leonard Smithers in February 1899 with the dedication to Alexander; the four-act manuscript was cut to three before the first night. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Lady Windermere's Fan: A Play About a Good Woman
description: First performed at the St James's Theatre on 20 February 1892, Wilde's first great social comedy and the play that made his name in the theatre: the story of a young wife's jealousy, a mother's sacrifice and a fan left in the wrong room.
plot_or_argument: Lady Windermere is about to leave her husband for Lord Darlington when Mrs Erlynne, a woman of doubtful reputation, intervenes; Mrs Erlynne is in fact Lady Windermere's mother, who left her husband and child twenty years before, and she sacrifices her own chance of respectability to save her daughter's marriage.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: Lady Windermere; Lord Windermere; Mrs Erlynne; Lord Darlington; the Duchess of Berwick; Lord Augustus Lorton; Cecil Graham; Lady Agatha Carlisle
literary_form: Play in four acts; problem play
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the doctrine of the 'woman with a past', the double standard, and the conventions of the well-made play. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1892 and first published in 1892 and first performed in St James's Theatre, London, 20 February 1892 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama; new woman and marriage-question novel.
literary_significance: Lady Windermere's Fan brought the moral question of the fallen woman onto the fashionable stage in a new key and established the formula of Wilde's social comedy: the society epigram enclosing a serious argument about forgiveness.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1892, as play in four acts, by Oscar Wilde. Composed between 1891 and 1892. First performed in St James's Theatre, London, 20 February 1892. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: An Ideal Husband
description: First performed at the Haymarket Theatre on 3 January 1895: the comedy of Sir Robert Chiltern, a rising politician whose career rests on a secret share-dealing of his youth, and of the blackmailer who threatens to expose him.
plot_or_argument: Mrs Cheveley, an adventuress, threatens to reveal that Chiltern sold a cabinet secret to Baron Arnheim; Chiltern's wife Gertrude demands that he resign, Lord Goring engineers the exposure of Mrs Cheveley, and the play ends with Chiltern's career intact and Goring engaged to Mabel Chiltern.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into four acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts on the well-made pattern: exposition, complication, the crisis of the argument, and the discovery that resolves it.
principal_characters: Sir Robert Chiltern; Lady Gertrude Chiltern; Lord Goring; Mrs Cheveley; Mabel Chiltern; Lord Caversham; Vicomte de Nanjac
literary_form: Play in four acts; problem play
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose: the dialogue carries everything, the acts are built on the well-made pattern of exposition, complication, crisis and discovery, and the argument is stated in set speeches and answered in the counter-speeches. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the politics of the Commons, financial speculation, and the public morality of the political career. The record dates the work as composed between 1894 and 1895 and first published in 1895 and first performed in Haymarket Theatre, London, 3 January 1895 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under problem play and well-made drama.
literary_significance: An Ideal Husband is Wilde's most political play: its subject is the relation between private corruption and public virtue, and its portrait of the blackmailing woman is one of the sharpest in the English theatre.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First produced at the Haymarket Theatre on 3 January 1895 and published by Leonard Smithers in 1899. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Salomé
description: Written in French in 1891 and published in Paris in 1893 with illustrations by Aubrey Beardsley; the English text appeared in 1894 with a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas. Banned from the London stage by the Lord Chamberlain, it was not performed in England until 1931.
plot_or_argument: Salomé, daughter of Herodias, desires the prophet Jokanaan (John the Baptist), who is imprisoned in Herod's cistern; when he rejects her, she demands his head on a silver charger as the price of dancing the dance of the seven veils, and at the end Herod orders her execution.
narrative_structure: The action is divided into one acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in blank verse, with the lyrical interludes and choruses set in shorter lines and in rhyme.
principal_characters: Salomé; Herod Antipas; Herodias; Jokanaan; the young Syrian; the Page of Herodias; Tigellinus
literary_form: Tragedy in one act (written in French)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Verse drama in blank verse: the unrhymed iambic pentameter carries the dialogue, with lyrical interludes in shorter lines and in rhyme for songs, choruses and set pieces. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The play is in a single act, played without interval. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the French symbolist theatre, the Decadent movement, and the censorship of the English stage. The record dates the work as composed between 1891 and 1893 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under victorian verse drama and revived tragedy; problem play and well-made drama.
literary_significance: Salomé is the central English text of dramatic decadence and the most influential one-act tragedy of the 1890s; its fusion of the biblical, the erotic and the aesthetic made it a scandal and a founding work of the modern theatre of cruelty.
attribution_notes: Written in French; the English version was a translation by Lord Alfred Douglas revised by Wilde.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1891, as tragedy in one act (written in french), by Oscar Wilde. Composed between 1891 and 1893. The original language is French (English translation 1894). The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: De Profundis
description: Written in Reading Gaol in early 1897 as a letter to Lord Alfred Douglas and published posthumously in 1905 in an abridged form; the complete text appeared in 1962. It is Wilde's confession, his defence and his most sustained work of prose.
plot_or_argument: The letter recounts the intimacy with Douglas, the quarrel and separation, the catastrophe of the trials, and the prison discipline of suffering; it ends with the resolution to accept the past and to return to art.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence.
literary_form: Epistolary essay (letter to Lord Alfred Douglas, written in Reading Gaol)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1895-97 imprisonment, the prison reform debates, and the aesthetic philosophy under the pressure of disgrace. The record dates the work as composed in 1897 and first published in 1905 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: De Profundis is the finest English prison narrative since the seventeenth century and the fullest statement of Wilde's late philosophy: that suffering is not to be escaped but understood, and that the artist's subject is his own life.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Written at Reading Gaol in 1897 and entrusted on release to Robert Ross; an abridged version was published by Methuen in 1905 and the full text, from the British Museum manuscript, first appeared in the Complete Letters of 1962. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Ballad of Reading Gaol
description: Published anonymously in 1898 under the prison number 'C.3.3.' and Wilde's last work: a ballad on the execution of Charles Thomas Wooldridge at Reading in 1896, and on the pity and horror of the common criminal's fate.
plot_or_argument: The ballad follows the prison routine, the condemned man's last days, the hanging, and the narrator's meditation on the shared guilt of all men; its refrain 'each man kills the thing he loves' made it one of the most quoted poems in English.
narrative_structure: An elegiac sequence: the stanzas repeat the mourning pattern, and the poem moves from the news of the death, through the lament and the questioning, to the consolation or the refusal of consolation.
principal_characters: the narrator; the condemned trooper, 'the man who had to swing'; the warders; the Chaplain; the Governor
literary_form: Ballad in six parts (published under the pseudonym C.3.3.)
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the elegiac mode: the mourning stanzas run in a repeated stanzaic pattern, the line is long enough to carry the lament and the apostrophe, and the movement is from grief to the consolation or the refusal of consolation that closes the sequence. The stanza is the ballad stanza, the four-stress and three-stress lines rhyming on the even lines. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the prison system, the campaign against capital punishment, and Wilde's own experience as prisoner C.3.3. The record dates the work as composed between 1897 and 1898 and first published in 1898 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under pastoral elegy and the mourning sequence; political verse and the poem of public cause.
literary_significance: The Ballad of Reading Gaol is the great English poem of prison reform and the last major Victorian poem; its refrain entered the language and its subject made it a founding text of the literature of incarceration.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Leonard Smithers on 13 February 1898 in an edition of 800 copies, under the prison number 'C.3.3.'; six editions ran off in the year and the author's name was added in the seventh. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
description: Published in 1888 and the first of Wilde's two collections of fairy tales: 'The Happy Prince', 'The Nightingale and the Rose', 'The Selfish Giant', 'The Devoted Friend' and 'The Remarkable Rocket'. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Oscar Wilde; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The swallow helps the gilded statue of the Happy Prince give away its jewels to the poor, and dies with it; the nightingale stains a white rose with its heart's blood for a student who will not be loved; the Selfish Giant is converted by a child, and in the last tale a conceited firework explodes to nothing.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: the Happy Prince; the Swallow; the Nightingale; the Student and the Professor's daughter; the Selfish Giant and the little boy; Little Hans and the Miller ('The Devoted Friend'); the Remarkable Rocket
literary_form: Fairy-tale collection; children's fantasy
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1880s, the Victorian fairy-tale revival, and the social misery of the 1880s that the tales address. The record dates the work as composed in 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade, it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: The Happy Prince is the finest English literary fairy tale of the century and one of the first children's books to make social justice its subject; its fusion of aesthetic beauty and Christian compassion is unique in the period.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by David Nutt in May 1888 with illustrations by Walter Crane and Jacomb Hood. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Intentions
description: Published in 1891 and collecting 'The Decay of Lying', 'Pen, Pencil and Poison', 'The Critic as Artist' and 'The Truth of Masks': the manifesto of English aesthetic criticism. It is a prose work of 1891 by Oscar Wilde; it belongs to Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade and it is catalogued here under Review Essay and Quarterly Argument; Lecture and Popular Address and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: 'The Decay of Lying' argues that life imitates art and that nature is a bad model; 'The Critic as Artist' makes criticism itself an art and the critic a creator; 'Pen, Pencil and Poison' treats the murderer Thomas Griffiths Wainewright as an artist in crime.
narrative_structure: An essay in sections, the argument stated, the evidence quoted, the objection answered and the judgement delivered, in the compass of the quarterly review. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
literary_form: Collection of critical dialogues and essays
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the quarterlies: the long periodic sentence of argument, the quotation and the set-piece judgement, the division into numbered or titled sections, and the assumption of a general reader of the reviewing class. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the inverted aphorism and the paradoxical epigram.
historical_context: The 1890s, the English reception of Pater, Ruskin and the French symbolists, and the periodical culture of the Fortnightly and the Nineteenth Century. The record dates the work as composed between 1889 and 1891 and first published in 1891 and the corpus places it within Aestheticism and the Decadent Decade; Arnold and the Criticism of Culture, it is catalogued under review essay and quarterly argument; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Intentions is the central text of English aesthetic criticism and the most brilliant polemic in Victorian criticism; its paradoxes about art and life shaped the theory of the modern novel and of the criticism of culture.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Oscar Fingal O'Flahertie Wills Wilde. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Osgood, McIlvaine in May 1891, collecting the dialogues and essays printed in the Nineteenth Century, the Woman's World and the Fortnightly Review between 1887 and 1891. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
description: Published in 1865 and told first to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat at Oxford on 4 July 1862: the founding work of English children's fantasy and the great Victorian book of nonsense. It is a prose fiction work of 1865 by Lewis Carroll; it is catalogued here under Children's Fantasy and the Dream-Region Tale; Nonsense Verse and the Parody of Rule and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Alice follows a White Rabbit down a hole into a world of talking animals, a Caterpillar with a hookah, a Cheshire Cat, a Mad Tea-Party, the Queen of Hearts and her croquet-ground, and a trial over stolen tarts; she wakes to find herself beside her sister on the bank.
narrative_structure: Twelve chapters, each built on a single encounter or a parodied verse, with Tenniel's illustrations as part of the text.
principal_characters: Alice; the White Rabbit; the Cheshire Cat; the Caterpillar; the Mad Hatter; the March Hare; the Queen of Hearts; the Duchess; the Mock Turtle; the Gryphon
literary_form: Children's fantasy novel (with illustrations by John Tenniel)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The text is written for children, the sentence short and the vocabulary plain. The author's characteristic manner is logical paradox, pun and wordplay.
historical_context: The 1860s, Oxford and Christ Church, the Victorian fashion for literary nonsense after Lear, and the golden age of the illustrated children's book. The record dates the work as composed between 1862 and 1865 and first published in 1865 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Alice is the founding text of modern children's fantasy and of English literary nonsense: its logic of the absurd, its parody of Victorian didacticism and its refusal to moralise changed what a book for children could be.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Macmillan in London in July 1865, the first edition of 2,000 copies being withdrawn because of the binder's complaint about the plates and reissued in November 1865; the illustrations are by John Tenniel. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There
description: Published in 1871 and generally thought the finer of the two Alice books: the mirror-world of chess, with its reversible logic, its chessboard landscape and its great inventions Tweedledum and Tweedledee and the Jabberwock.
plot_or_argument: Alice climbs through the drawing-room mirror into a country laid out as a chessboard and plays her way from pawn to queen; she meets the Red Queen, Tweedledum and Tweedledee, Humpty Dumpty, the White Knight, and wakes as she takes the Red Queen's crown.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: Alice; the Red Queen; the White Queen; Humpty Dumpty; Tweedledum; Tweedledee; the White Knight; the Jabberwock; Haigha; Hatta
literary_form: Children's fantasy novel (with illustrations by John Tenniel)
meter_and_prosody: Prose narrative interspersed with parodic verse ('Jabberwocky', 'The Walrus and the Carpenter', 'A-Sitting on a Gate').
historical_context: The 1860s-70s, the game of chess and the algebra of symbols, and the Victorian interest in mirror imagery and reversibility. The record dates the work as composed between 1869 and 1871 and first published in 1871 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Through the Looking-Glass is the most formally perfect children's book in English: its chess structure, its mirror logic and its invented vocabulary ('Jabberwocky', 'chortle', 'galumphing') gave the language new words and the modern literature of the absurd its method.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1871, by Lewis Carroll. Composed between 1869 and 1871. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Hunting of the Snark: An Agony in Eight Fits
alternative_titles: Hunting of the Snark: An Agony in Eight Fits
description: Published in 1876 and the greatest long nonsense poem in English: the voyage of a Bellman, a Baker, a Butcher, a Barrister, a Billiard-marker, a Banker, a Beaver, a Boots and a Bonnet-maker in search of a creature that may not exist.
plot_or_argument: The crew sails with a map that is a blank, a rule that the Snark may be a Boojum, and the Baker's warning that if the Snark is a Boojum he will 'softly and suddenly vanish away'; the Baker finds the Snark, discovers it is a Boojum, and vanishes.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
principal_characters: The Bellman; the Baker; the Butcher; the Barrister; the Banker; the Beaver; the Billiard-marker; the Boots; the Bonnet-maker
literary_form: Nonsense poem in eight fits; nonsense verse
meter_and_prosody: Fourteen-line stanzas of anapaestic tetrameter and trimeter with the rhyme-scheme of 'The Lady of Shalott'.
historical_context: The 1870s, the Victorian culture of exploration and classification, and the philosophical debate about the reality of the external world. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1876 and first published in 1876 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; children's fantasy and the dream-region tale.
literary_significance: The Hunting of the Snark is the most philosophically serious nonsense poem in English: it is at once an allegory of scientific pursuit, of the search for meaning and of the fear of annihilation, and it has never been fully explained, which is its point.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Macmillan in London in March 1876, with illustrations by Henry Holiday. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Phantasmagoria and Other Poems
description: Published in 1869 and Carroll's first collection of verse, including the title poem 'Phantasmagoria' — a comic dialogue between a ghost and the man he haunts — and 'The Sea-Bathing' and 'A Sea Dirge'.
plot_or_argument: 'Phantasmagoria' stages a conversation between a spectre and an unimpressed householder about the rules of haunting, the etiquette of ghosts and the tedium of the profession; the shorter poems move between parody, sentiment and logical joke.
narrative_structure: A collection of short comic pieces, each complete in its stanza form and each turning on the same joke of exact rule and absurd sense.
literary_form: Poetry collection; nonsense verse
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of regular comic metre: the limerick, the double dactyl, the ballad stanza and the parody of a received form, with the rhyme exact and the sense deliberately absurd. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is logical paradox, pun and wordplay.
historical_context: The 1860s, the Victorian vogue for spiritualism and the ghost story, and the Punch tradition of comic verse. The record dates the work as composed between 1860 and 1869 and first published in 1869 and it is catalogued under nonsense verse and the parody of rule; ghost story and scientific supernatural tale.
literary_significance: Phantasmagoria is the best comic ghost poem in English and shows Carroll's method at its most characteristic: the application of strict logic to an impossible premise.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1869, as poetry collection, by Lewis Carroll. Composed between 1860 and 1869. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Sylvie and Bruno
description: Published in 1889 and the strangest of Carroll's books: a double narrative that alternates between the fairy world of Elfland, ruled by the Warden and the Chancellor, and the Victorian country house of the real world.
plot_or_argument: The narrator moves between the fairy kingdom of Sylvie and Bruno and the English world of Lady Muriel and Arthur Forester; the fairy plot turns on the Warden's abdication and the usurping Chancellor, the real plot on a love affair and a death, and the two are linked by the narrator's trances.
narrative_structure: A story for children in short chapters, each of one sitting's length, the marvel named and repeated so that the child can follow it.
principal_characters: Sylvie; Bruno; the narrator; Lady Muriel Orme; Arthur Forester; Eric Lindon; the Earl, Lady Muriel's father; the Warden; the Sub-Warden and my Lady; Uggug; the Professor; the Other Professor
literary_form: Fantasy novel (with illustrations by Harry Furniss)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose for children: the plain declarative sentence, the direct address to the reader, the named and repeating marvel, and the short chapter pitched to the reading aloud of a single sitting. The text was issued with illustrations, which carry part of the meaning. The author's characteristic manner is logical paradox, pun and wordplay.
historical_context: The 1880s, Carroll's later interest in logic, spiritualism and social reform, and the Victorian fairy painting of Richard Dadd and Joseph Noel Paton. The record dates the work as composed between 1874 and 1889 and first published in 1889 and it is catalogued under children's fantasy and the dream-region tale; nonsense verse and the parody of rule.
literary_significance: Sylvie and Bruno is the most ambitious and least successful of Carroll's fantasies, but it is a key text for the late-Victorian fairy revival and for the study of the double narrative in children's fiction.
attribution_notes: It was published under the name Lewis Carroll, one of the author's pseudonyms; the attribution to Lewis Carroll is secure. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1889, as fantasy novel (with illustrations by harry furniss), by Lewis Carroll. Composed between 1874 and 1889. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Dracula
description: Published on 26 May 1897 and the most influential horror novel ever written: the story of the Transylvanian Count who comes to England to found a new empire of the undead, and of the small company that hunts him down.
plot_or_argument: Jonathan Harker visits Count Dracula in Transylvania and escapes; the Count ships to Whitby, where Lucy Westenra is drained and dies, and Mina Harker is bitten; Van Helsing, Seward, Holmwood and Morris pursue the Count back to Transylvania and destroy him at his castle.
narrative_structure: Epistolary collage of journals, letters, telegrams and newspaper cuttings, with Mina's typescript as the organising document.
principal_characters: Count Dracula; Jonathan Harker; Mina Harker; Lucy Westenra; Abraham Van Helsing; John Seward; Arthur Holmwood; Quincey Morris; Renfield
literary_form: Epistolary novel; ghost story
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the supernatural: the rational first-person witness, the exact circumstantial detail that makes the impossible credible, the withheld explanation, and the closing sentence that leaves the reader with the horror unaccounted for. The text is cast as letters, the argument carried by correspondence. The author's characteristic manner is epistolary and documentary collage.
